scenes.title: How calculus connects motion

beats.text: Velocity is displacement changing with time: d s by d t.
Acceleration is velocity changing with time: d v by d t.
Reverse by integration: integrate acceleration for velocity, velocity for displacement.
A curved velocity graph has changing acceleration. Constant acceleration formulae fail.
beats.caption: Changing gradient means changing acceleration.

scenes.title: Find both integration constants

beats.text: Consider a trolley speeding up to the right. Find its velocity and position.
Right is positive. Acceleration is six t plus two metres per second squared.
Initially its velocity is four metres per second.
It starts one metre right of the origin: s at zero is positive one.
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
Integrating six t plus two gives three t squared plus two t plus C.
Use the initial velocity: four equals C.
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
Integrating gives t cubed plus t squared plus four t plus D.
At zero, s is positive one, so D equals one.
Start on the negative side instead? D becomes minus one; velocity stays unchanged.
beats.caption: Position needs a stated sign.

scenes.title: Follow the particle first

beats.text: Consider a particle leaving the origin, moving right. It slows down as it travels.
It stops for an instant, then turns back. Its velocity becomes negative.
It returns to the origin and stops again. We will find when it turns, and how far it travels.

scenes.title: Rest and acceleration

beats.text: Velocity is three t squared minus twelve t plus nine metres per second.
Use zero to three seconds.
Initially s is zero. Find the first rest time and acceleration.
Instantaneous rest means velocity equals zero.
Substitute the given velocity: three t squared minus twelve t plus nine equals zero.
Factorise: three times t minus one times t minus three equals zero.
Rest at one and three seconds; first at one.
For acceleration, differentiate velocity. A equals d v by d t.
This gives six t minus twelve metres per second squared. Acceleration changes with time.

scenes.title: Displacement and its graph

beats.text: Find displacement and sketch its graph, using the same givens.
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
Substitute three t squared minus twelve t plus nine.
Integrating term by term gives t cubed minus six t squared plus nine t plus C.
At time zero, displacement is zero, so C is zero. Show this step.
Now the displacement time graph. It rises from zero to four metres as the particle moves right.
Then it falls to zero as the particle returns. The horizontal tangents mark the two instants of rest.

scenes.title: Read velocity, then count both legs

beats.text: Now the velocity time graph: nine initially, zero at one second and three seconds.
Signed displacement is the integral of velocity. Distance adds leg magnitudes.
For the outward leg, evaluate t cubed minus six t squared plus nine t, from zero to one.
That gives four metres out.
For the return leg, evaluate the same expression from one to three.
Minus four metres: the particle travels back.
Distance equals the magnitude of the first displacement plus the magnitude of the second.
Four plus the magnitude of minus four gives eight metres. Net displacement is zero.
Average speed equals distance divided by time.
Eight divided by three is two point six seven metres per second.
Average velocity uses displacement over time, so it is zero.

scenes.title: Check maximum speed

beats.text: For maximum speed, compare velocity magnitudes at stationary velocity points and endpoints.
beats.caption: Compare |v|: stationary points and endpoints.

beats.text: Here, acceleration equals zero at two seconds, where velocity is minus three.
Is that the maximum speed? Compare it with the endpoints.
beats.caption: Is the stationary value the maximum speed?

beats.text: No. Compare speeds: nine initially, three at the stationary point, zero finally. Maximum speed: nine metres per second.
You can now differentiate motion functions.
